thread_title: S. leucophylla var. alba Washington Co, AL
breadcrumb: S. leucophylla var. alba Washington Co, AL

posts.body_html:
Another super crazy white clone! Edit:this thread is to cover multiple different alba clones from Washington Co, AL... I'm starting to think that these very bright white genes are recessive because a couple of the absolutely brightest white clones I have are not very vigorous (ie. Mike King's S. leucophylla var. alba MKL042). Low vigor suggests the individuals are the result of selfing somewhere down the line and with selfing, you tend to see a lot more recessive genes show up in the phenotype. To support this hypothesis, albas in the wild in general are relatively rare and uncommon even in large stands of S. leucophylla.

Here's yet another blindingly white clone of S. leucophylla var. alba Washington Co, AL. Photos taken 6/17/16:




much like hurricane creek white, this individual can have red pigments in the traps under certain environmental conditions:

posts.body_html:
I think we can comfortably say that these rival hurricane creek white in white-ness and beauty. Let's not also forget, they can produce incredible summer traps too, unlike many other leucophylla clones/populations.

Some new photos of S. leucophylla var. alba Washington Co, Al, taken 7/21/16:



Back view:





These two traps are from the same exact plant! I've had albas that produced "non-alba" looking traps during the spring, only to spit out solid bright white fall traps! In this case below, a bright white trap shot out, followed by a somewhat regular looking trap. It's really confusing and weird:

It's hammer time...er LEUCO TIME baby! This year we're seeing some very early fall pitcher production, and it makes me wonder if this is it, or if they're going to continue producing. For sure, some will keep going, but will the ones that have already produced big fall traps produce even more?

New photos, taken 8/15/16:



love the look of this one:



Not all of these are from Washington Co, AL, but they are all proven albas. Some look like normal leucos, but don't be fooled, it's just phenotypic variation:

posts.body_html: Here's a S. leucophylla var. alba that looks like hurricane creek white (HCW), but it's not (at least in my book). Unfortunately, the cultivar description for HCW allows plants like these to be called HCW...too bad it doesn't specify that the cutivar has to come directly from the now destoyed site near Hurricane creek in Baldwin Co, AL. Oh gosh, looks like this clone just got a new name, S. leucophylla var. alba 'HCW imposter' Washington Co, AL, LOL! Photos taken 9/15/16:
